newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia landslide toll at six, survivor holds on.
newsitem.headline: Australia landslide toll at six, survivor holds on.

text.p: The only known survivor of a landslide at an Australian ski resort remained entombed on Saturday more than 10 hours after his miraculous discovery under tonnes of rubble, and the official death toll rose to six.
As rescue crews continued the slow and dangerous task of digging the man from the mass of concrete, steel and mud, officials announced the discovery of more bodies.
The confirmed dead include four men and two women, a police spokeswoman said. Only one body has been recovered.
Thirteen people are still missing following the landslide which engulfed two ski lodges at Thredbo Alpine Village, about 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney.
"There were six dead at the latest count," the police spokeswoman told Reuters. Previously, police had put the confirmed death toll at three.
Rescuers were speaking to the survivor, identified as ski instructor Stuart Diver, and one was able to hold his hand through a small hole in the cavity where he was trapped.
Rescuers also managed to feed him a liquid nutrient solution and warm air was being pumped into the space.
"All reports are that he is in great spirits," ambulance spokesman Dane Goodwin told reporters.
"He has been able to move his arms around so we believe it's like a mini-tomb in there."
Rescue officials said he appeared to be suffering from lacerations and hypothermia.
Police chief superintendent Charlie Sanderson told Reuters one of the bodies was found near Diver.
Diver's wife Sally was one of the 20 people buried in the slide which hit the lodges in the Snowy Mountains.
"We are assuming that there is a body in where Stuart is, and that is pretty well for certain, but we don't know who it is," Sanderson told Reuters.
Earlier, rescuers made contact with Diver, who has survived more than 64 hours entombed between huge concrete slabs.
Rescuers said the recovery process was slow because of the dangers of another slide and slippage of debris.
"It is being pulled away inch by inch. We have had to make sure we don't allow this slab to move. It is a frustrating, slow process," Fire Brigade spokesman Ian Krimmer told reporters.
"We are discussing quite freely with him. He is able to describe to us the feelings, what he is hearing, which is a good sign for us," Krimmer said.
"There is a lot of comforting being given to him. We have to make sure that we maintain his morale in this situation."
Rescuers managed to feed Diver a warm solution of electrolytes and nutrients, a police spokeswoman said.
"They managed to pass a small torch (flashlight) through to the man and it has enabled him to describe his present situation to the rescue team," she said.
Krimmer said rescuers believed the area where the man was found may be a bedroom, as mattresses and blankets had been recovered, suggesting others may still be found.
"We are in an area now where there is a chance of other survivors," Krimmer said.
"So from time to time you are seeing equipment being shut down, so we can utilise our seismic listening devices."
Police had virtually ruled out the chance of finding a survivor, but just before dawn on Saturday rescuers heard muffled sounds and detected muscle movement under a concrete slab.
Fireman Steve Hirst was the first to speak with Diver after calling for silence at the rescue scene after hearing a noise.
"I got the chainsaw knocked off and went down on my stomach and made contact. I yelled out: 'Rescue team working overhead, can anyone hear me'," Hirst said.
"I repeated the call and had a voice come strongly back to me," he said.
The trapped man's first words were: "I can hear you."
